q: The principle of superposition of waves states that the resultant displacement at a point is
o: always zero when two waves meet
the average of the individual displacements
the algebraic sum of the individual displacements
why: Superposition: y(resultant) = y1 + y2 + y3 + ... (algebraic sum)

q: In a stationary wave y = 2A cos(omega t) sin(kx), the distance between two successive nodes is
why: In a stationary wave, adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by lambda/2

q: At a node in a stationary wave, the amplitude of vibration is
o: equal to the amplitude of one wave A
why: Nodes are points of permanent zero displacement in a stationary wave

q: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string of length L under tension T and mass per unit length m is
why: Fundamental frequency of a string: n = (1/2L) sqrt(T/m)

q: An open organ pipe of length L produces a fundamental frequency given by
why: Open pipe fundamental frequency: n = v/2L, and it supports all harmonics

q: A closed organ pipe of length L supports which harmonics?
why: A closed pipe (one end closed) produces only odd harmonics, with fundamental n = v/4L

q: If two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together, the beat frequency heard is
Beats are produced due to the superposition of two sound waves having
o: the same frequency and same phase
why: Beats arise from superposition of two waves with slightly different frequencies, causing periodic amplitude variation

q: The end correction in a resonance tube experiment accounts for the fact that
o: the antinode forms exactly at the open end
the tube has no effect on resonance
sound travels faster inside the tube
the antinode forms slightly outside the open end of the tube
why: Due to edge effects, the antinode actually lies slightly above the open end, requiring an end correction

q: In a resonance tube experiment, if L2 and L1 are two successive resonance lengths, the speed of sound is given by
why: Since L2 - L1 = lambda/2, speed v = n lambda = 2n(L2 - L1)
